blindSummary:
This country is authoritarian but not criminalising. The most directly visitor-specific finding is airport discrimination: a transgender video creator from a country in the region was singled out and subjected to discriminatory treatment at an airport here. The most severe documented case is forced psychiatric commitment: a trans woman was held for 97 days and subjected to electroshock "conversion" therapy under family pressure (she won unprecedented compensation), showing the medical/psychiatric system can be weaponized — though this targeted a resident, not a tourist.

Under the current leadership, the space for LGBTQ+ organising and expression is shrinking: Pride-month social-media and film censorship, a government crackdown on LGBT NGOs (2023), a performance ban on a famous transgender television personality, and cancellation of a foreign drag performer's tour. There is no criminalisation of trans identity, no bathroom restriction law, and courts can provide some protection, but there are no anti-discrimination protections.

This country is a regional hub for gender-affirming care, but the parental-consent barrier applies even to adults.
blindOutOfScope: General state surveillance, internet censorship, and arbitrary-detention risks affect all travellers here; only trans-specific risk is assessed.
blindSourceSummaries: Foreign news site (May 2025): a renowned trans video creator from a country in the region accused immigration officers of sexist, mocking treatment during a family trip - officers laughed at and questioned her at an airport in this country. Directly relevant to trans travellers' airport experiences here.
NOTE: not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying investigation (Dec 2024) by an international daily covers transgender 'conversion' practices in this country.

Foreign broadsheet (Nov 2024): a performance artist, 28, won a record payout after being subjected to electroshock 'conversion' treatment - the first time a trans person won such a case in this country; she hoped the case would help other LGBTQ+ people protect their rights.
An international rights group (Jun 2026): social-media posts and films with LGBT-related content were censored in this country around Pride month.

Foreign-funded broadcaster (Jan 2024): the ruling party continues a crackdown on LGBTQ+ people as part of a campaign against 'foreign ideologies' - public display of rainbow flags banned, activism 'all but extinct' within the country, in contrast to a nearby jurisdiction's 2019 marriage equality; queer and trans people report growing abuse.

A foreign-policy magazine feature (Jan 2025): gender transition in this country is treated as a family matter — gender-affirming surgery is conditioned on parental consent and family involvement, with new rules restricting access.

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): the official line of neither encouraging, opposing nor promoting LGBTQ+ existence has become increasingly restrictive - cybersecurity legislation enables censorship of LGBTIQ content; in 2025 several gay dating apps were removed from a major app store and prominent queer accounts forced to rebrand or shut down; most advocacy organisations have closed or gone underground; narrow 'family values' pressure intensifies.
A cable-news report (Jan 2025): cancellations of the shows of a celebrated transgender media figure feed fears of a wider LGBTQ+ crackdown in this country.
International news service: a drag performer from abroad faces repression here - reporting on the treatment of a gender-nonconforming performer in this country.
A cable-news report (Mar 2016): this country's broadcast regulator banned depictions of same-sex romance on television as 'abnormal sexual behaviour'.
blindLocalsOnly: Legal gender recognition requires surgery and parental consent at any age — a resident-facing regime; the forced psychiatric commitment case targeted a resident; the regional gender-affirming-care hub status and its parental-consent barrier concern residents seeking care.
